title: An iconic 1960s UFO-like prefabricated house is brought back to life
excerpt: The Space Age aesthetic is back in fashion, and at the same time, there’s a new appreciation of craftsmanship. The two come together with Matti Suuronen’s Futuro House recently recreated in Helsinki.
content:
The prefabricated Futuro House, in its 2026 edition, reflects a broader trend. Nostalgia for the 1960s and 1970s is sweeping across everything from fashion to music—and design is no exception. Contemporary creations by the French designer Axel Chay, Gustaf Westman in Sweden, and the French collective Uchronia celebrate whimsical, colorful forms infused with an exuberant Space Age spirit. First emerging in the late 1950s with the fascination around the space race, and coinciding with the postwar rise of prefabricated architecture, the playful Space Age aesthetic has a lightheartedness that’s often lacking in other styles. It’s within this global context that Matti Suuronen’s Futuro House—presented during this year’s Helsinki Design Week by the Finnish brand Marimekko—was revived.

A Very 1960s Design

The original Futuro House was created in fibreglass by the Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in 1968. Born shortly before the Second World War, Suuronen’s goal was to create a prefabricated ski chalet that was lightweight and which could be assembled without much effort, but that would also be easy to heat (given the local temperatures in Finland) and adaptable to any type of terrain. His style was very much in keeping with the spirit of the times, when tournesol piscines (domed sunflower swimming pools) were appearing across France and “bubble houses” resembling UFOs were springing up around the world. The elliptical shape of the Futuro House thus reflects both technical advances and post-war trends centred on fantasies around nuclear power, space exploration and material innovations—at the time, plastic, plywood and aluminium were all inexpensive and being mass-produced at new scales.

Designed to be mass produced, like many other similar projects of the 1960s from large-scale housing estates to Japanese Metabolist capsules, around 100 Futuro Houses were erected worldwide. Production came to a halt when the oil crises of the following decade brought the reign of plastic to an end; yet, when Suuronen died in 2013, there were still around 60 surviving models. The Futuro House was dormant and waiting to be brought back to life.

The Futuro House Enthusiast Behind its Recent Revival

This is where architect Jan van Dijs enters the story. While disposable materials such as PVC are no longer in vogue in 2020, the modularity and compact design of the Futuro House—a forerunner of the current tiny house phenomenon—are more appealing than ever. This is what led this American fan of Space Age design to research architects of the period. Having fallen in love with Suuronen’s prefabricated house, van Dijs set about searching for moulds with the aim of reproducing it. The existing ones, however, were in poor condition and he needed the consent of the late architect’s descendants to create new moulds. Undeterred, van Dijs contacted the Suuronen family, as well as former manufacturers, and embarked on a daring project: to rebuild the Futuro House entirely by hand, faithful to its original specifications—a single-piece moulded structure made of plastic and fibreglass, and then painted white.

Following the complex process involved with recreating the Futuro House, the team behind the project then set about designing interiors that also faithfully reproduced the original, working from Suuronen’s drawings. A handful of distinctly Space Age-style plastic pieces punctuate the open-plan areas of the tiny space: a kitchen and dining area, a living area and a bedroom. The structure has 25 square metres of floor space, while the area at its widest point is nearly 50 square metres (the difference is the result of the elliptical shape of the house). Suuronen’s descendants at the unveiling of the 2026 version in Helsinki recalled, “We used to spend holidays in this house, which may have been small but was very practical.”

Marimekko Textiles Add a 2026 Touch

While given its small size, it can accommodate only a few guests at a time, the Futuro House nevertheless impresses with its functional, whimsical and light-filled interiors, now enhanced by contributions from Marimekko (the only contemporary touches added to the project). The iconic Finnish brand became involved after construction was complete, upholstering the furniture in striped fabrics by textile artist-in-residence Vibeke Rohland and also supplying tableware. The colourful additions enhance the inherent joy of this house, which resembles a UFO from the outside and the set of a 1960s James Bond film on the inside.
